text: This capstone starts the same way most real security work does -- not as a fully scoped engagement, but as one worried sentence from one manager.

You're three weeks into your first job as a Security Analyst at Hartwell Regional Utilities, a mid-size regional electric and water utility. Dale Granger, the IT Manager, catches you by the break room. He says: we had a close one last week, someone in Billing almost clicked a phishing link, caught it at the last second, more luck than process. I don't want to find out the hard way next time. Can you tighten things up, and if something does get through, let me actually know about it.

That sentence is really two asks glued together. Tighten things up -- every server, or a slice? What does hardened even mean? And know about it -- know about what, specifically? A detection rule tuned to catch everything catches nothing reliably.

A short follow-up conversation gets four concrete answers: scope -- two Windows servers and two Linux servers, not the whole environment. Baseline -- a documented standard, not a personal judgment call. Detection target -- a cluster of failed sign-ins followed by a success, the exact pattern a phished credential would produce if it got used. And deliverable -- a reusable checklist plus one working rule Mara can actually demonstrate.

Scoping also means saying what's out of bounds. This project skips a full penetration test, skips every server Hartwell runs, and skips a full SOC build-out with dozens of rules. One well-chosen detection rule, done properly, on a representative handful of servers, is the actual ask.
With the requirement written down, next lesson turns it into a real baseline hardening checklist -- picking a recognized standard and scoping exactly which checks apply to these four servers.
